newsitem.title: USA: Mass. wrestles with budget, bonds and benefits.
newsitem.headline: Mass. wrestles with budget, bonds and benefits.

text.p: Massachusetts legislators will this week wrestle with such issues as the 1998 budget, how to pay for the Big Dig and extending health benefits to gays and lesbians.

The House Ways and Means Committee is expected to conclude its hearings Thursday on the $18.4 billion budget submitted by Gov. William Weld. In contrast to earlier years, Democrats in the Legislature were quoted last week as saying the Republican governor's budget may be as much as $100 million out of balance and overly generous.

Ways and Means Committee chairman Paul Haley, D-Weymouth, and House Speaker Thomas Finneran, D-Mattapan, warned that while revenues this fiscal year are running about 9.0 percent above Fiscal 1997 estimates, Fiscal 1998, which starts July 1, may not be so robust. Senate, House and Weld administration officials are expected to meet Tuesday to get down to specifics.

The measure granting authority to raise money for the Third Harbor Tunnel/Central Artery Project, also known as the Big Dig, by diverting money from state authorities and raising tolls on the harbor crossings and Massachusetts Turnpike could also come before the House this week. The state needs to have a plan in place by April 1 to pay its approximately 25 percent share of the $10.7 billion to be spent on what is being called the nation's largest construction project.

A legislative working group's report on how to pay for a new Boston convention center is expected by the end of the week, but may be delayed a few days. A team of experts issued a preliminary report on the center in January and estimated the cost at $695 million.

There is an expectation that the working group will recommend some hike in the Boston hotel tax to help pay for the facility. Other options expected in special earmarking of sales taxes in the area around the convention center; hikes in Logan Airport fees; and charging developers for the right to build near the new center.

Officials from fiscally challenged Middlesex County, home to both Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, are expected in state court Wednesday to answer a lawsuit filed against them by several creditors. The county defaulted on $4.5 million in loans and is close to $17 million in debt. State legislators are holding another hearing on the matter Tuesday.

Also Tuesday, the Public Service Committee will take up measures affecting group insurance and leave benefits for public employes. The highlight is a bill filed by Rep. Byron Rushing and Rep. Paul Demakis, both Boston Democrats, extending health insurance and other benefits to the domestic partners of gays and lesbians who work for state government.
